items.title: Plea in Karnataka High Court challenges State order on singing only 2 stanzas of Vande Mataram
items.summary: A Public Interest Litigation (PIL) petition has been filed before the Karnataka High Court against State government‘s recent order mandating that only first two stanzas of national song Vande Mataram be sung at State functions [Girish Bharadwaj v State of Karnataka] . The PIL has been filed by advocate Girish Bharadwaj who will be represented by advocate Angad Kamath. It is likely to be mentioned for an urgent hearing on Wednesday. On September 8, the State government mandated that only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram be sung at State government functions. The order, however, provides an exception for programmes where the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister or Governor are in attendance and permits all 6 stanzas be sung in such programmes. Stating that the Parliament recently enacted the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, 2026 to include Vande Mataram as a national song and provide it with similar status as the national anthem, the PIL contends that the government order has undermined the parliament's intent to protect the full version of the song. items.title: What is your source? Delhi HC on plea alleging people still trapped under Satya Niketan building debris
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Monday took exception to a plea alleging that people could still be trapped underneath the debris of the Satya Niketan building that collapsed on September 6 leading to the death of seven people. The plea was mentioned for urgent listing before a bench of Chief Justice (CJ) Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia . The plea claimed that the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) demolished a building adjoining the collapsed Satya Niketan building without clearing the debris, and that there may be people still trapped inside. However, the Court asked the petitioner's counsel what the urgency was and also demanded what the source of his information was. "What is your source of information that there are people below the debris? How do you know?" the CJ demanded. The Court said that the authorities must have conducted some technical audit before demolishing the adjoining building. CJ Upadhyaya told the petitioner to file the plea, adding that it will be auto-listed. "They must have conducted some type of technical audit before deciding to demolish. Collector of Pune & Anr.]. Additional Government Pleader KB Dighe informed the court that September 25 shall be observed as a ‘dry day’ and prohibition on retail liquor sale will operate on September 14 till 4 pm. A division bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait M Sethna had earlier slammed the blanket prohibition on liquor for 10 days. Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna “What is the rationale behind choosing only Pune? We deprecate such practice," Chief Justice Tripathi said. He cautioned that sudden alcohol deprivation could send habitual drinkers into physical shock and lead to hospital admissions. The Court was hearing a plea by National Restaurant Association of India and retail liquor associations challenging the original 10-day prohibition. items.title: Justice V Kameswar Rao takes over as Chief Justice of Patna High Court
items.summary: Justice V Kameswar Rao on Sunday took oath as the Chief Justice of Patna High Court. Justice Rao was administered the oath of office by Bihar Governor Lt. Gen. Syed Ata Hasnain (Retd). Justice Rao, originally a judge of the Delhi High Court, was recommended for elevation as the Chief Justice by the Supreme Court Collegium on August 6. The appointment was notified by the Central government on September 05. Justice V Kameswar Rao Justice Rao did his LLB from Delhi University in 1990. He enrolled as an advocate in March 1991. Following years of practice, he was elevated as an additional judge of the Delhi High Court in April 2013 and was made permanent in March 2015. He was transferred to the Karnataka High Court in 2024. He served as acting Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court in May 2025. He was repatriated to the Delhi High Court on July 21, 2025. items.title: Teacher hitting girl students on back, waist without sexual intent not offence under POCSO Act: Supreme Court
items.summary: The Supreme Court has recently quashed a case under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act) against a school teacher accused of hitting minor girl students on their back and waist during class [Bhaskar Paul v. State of West Bengal]. In an order passed on September 8, a bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar held that the students’ statements did not indicate that the teacher had touched them with sexual intent, which is necessary to constitute sexual assault under the POCSO Act. The Court acknowledged that the teacher’s use of corporal punishment was inappropriate and that he should have been more sensitive while dealing with girl students. However, it said that such conduct alone could not justify prosecuting him for aggravated sexual assault under the POCSO Act. items.title: Regulating arbitrators like Supreme Court, High Court judges is impossible: Retired Justice AK Sikri
items.summary: It would be impossible to regulate arbitrators in exactly the same manner as Supreme Court and High Court judges, former Supreme Court Justice AK Sikri said during a debate at India ADR Week 2026. Justice Sikri was one of the judges for the Oxford-style debate on whether arbitrators should be professionally regulated like judges. Judging the debate along him were Dentons Link Legal Managing Partner Atul Sharma and Carsten van de Sande of Hengeler Mueller. The debate was moderated by Saraf & Partners partner Sanya Sud . Justice Sikri said that the proposition itself could be understood in two ways: either that arbitrators should be subject to some form of regulation similar to judges, or that they should be regulated through the same mechanisms applicable to judges. If the latter interpretation were adopted, the proposition would fail, he said. “As I understood the parties and both the sides kept in mind the higher judicial service only, that is High Court and Supreme Court judges. items.title: Retired Justice Hima Kohli calls for statutory protection of government officers releasing disputed funds
items.summary: A statutory framework for interim payments in construction disputes can protect government and PSU officials who release contested funds from vigilance, audit and investigative scrutiny, former Supreme Court Justice Hima Kohli said during the Delhi leg of India ADR Week 2026. Justice Kohli said that officers often avoid taking commercial decisions on disputed payments because the responsibility for releasing public money falls directly on them. “ Keeping in mind that 70% or more of Indian infrastructure involves government agencies and PSUs, statutory backing becomes essential. In PSUs and government bodies, individual officers are hesitant to release disputed interim funds on their own discretion because the responsibility and scrutiny fall directly on their shoulders. A statute provides statutory cover and institutional protection to these officers, mandating interim payments under a clear legal procedure rather than leaving them vulnerable to accusations of impropriety, ” she said. She added that without such statutory backing, officers may prefer to push disputes into prolonged arbitration rather than take a commercial call to release funds and keep project cash flow moving. items.title: Legal Notes by Arvind Datar: Retrospectivity v. retroactivity and the need for a clear distinction
items.summary: What is the difference between a retrospective and a retroactive law? As this important question remains unanswered till date, this article suggests what the proper tests should be. Although most laws are prospective, it is settled that Parliament and the State legislatures have the competence to make laws with retrospective effect. These laws are declared to have come into effect on a date that is before the date of its enactment. Some laws have been declared to be effective decades earlier. The Finance Act, 1981 amended certain excise law provisions from 1944, while amendments made by the Finance Act, 2012 were to be effective from April 1, 2012. A “retroactive” law is also a law that is declared to be operative from an earlier date, but this category has a vital difference that is discussed a little later. The Supreme Court has referred to the two categories in several decisions. However, there is no clear distinction made in any of them. [See Shanti Conductors v. Assam State Electricity Board (2019) ; Shanti Conductors v. Assam State Electricity Board (2016) ; Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma, (2020) ; SEBI v. Rajkumar Nagpal (2023) ; Jay Mahakali Rolling Mills v. Union of India
